> >
> > Dear Kata,
> >
> > Regarding the $K.by.p results, make sure your choose verbose = TRUE in the function arguments.  That might not be abundantly clear in the help file, but the default is verbose = FALSE, which limits how many results to append to the object you make, to save memory.
> >
> > Regarding the results, the two optimization methods could be quite different, and to be honest, this is an area that requires better research.  The “mean” option allows each shape variable to have separate lambda values and is optimized, variable by variable, finding the mean lambda as a summary statistic.  The burn option requires each variable to have the same lambda but seeks to find the value of lambda that produces the highest log-likelihood, before finding an effect size for that lambda.  These are essentially different approaches, so different results should be expected.  One has to decide beforehand whether variables can have independent optimizations or whether an attribute, like shape, has to have the same lambda for every variable.
> >
> > Best,
> > Mike

> > > > El 19 feb. 2024, a las 11:06, Mike Collyer <mlco...@gmail.com> escribió:
> > > >
> > > > Hi María,
> > > >
> > > > If you wish to measure phylogenetic signal and use an effect size based on the log-likelihood, you might want to trim the dimensions of the data, since you have more variables than observations.  Maybe try using the first 21 or 22 PAC scores (and be prepared to cull further), rather than the coordinates (can do this in the arguments, with PAC.no) or use a higher value for the tolerance (change tol in the arguments).  The warning is indicating that there were instances where NA values were found for the log-likelihood, caused by ill-conditioned residual covariance matrices, which are typical if they are near singular (always the case if variable number and observation number are about the same).
> > > >
> > > > This is a difficult issue to anticipate and write a better warning for, but something we attempt to explain in the help file.  Because PACA concentrates phylogenetic signal in fewer dimensions than PCA, you can probably be reassured that using even a few dimensions is probably okay for your inferences about phylogenetic signal; i.e., if you repeat the analysis with say10, 11, 12, … maybe 20 PACs, you probably get similar z scores as results.  If it were me, I might explore what the results are with different numbers of PACs and find a place where the Z score seems stable but I do not risk bad log-likelihood estimated with too many PACs.
> > > >
> > > > Best,
> > > > Mike

> > > > > > > > > > El 1 feb. 2024, a las 12:01, Samuel Ginot <gino...@gmail.com> escribió:
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > Dear all,
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > I recently came across some discrepancy using the bilat.symmetry function with and without RRPP. I’d like to clarify whether this may be a bug, or if there is some sense to be made out of it. The following lines of code provide a reproducible case (geomorph version 4.0.4, RRPP version 1.3.0):
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > #-------------------------------------------------------
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > library(geomorph)
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > data(lizards)
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > gdf <- geomorph.data.frame(shape = lizards$coords, ind = lizards$ind, replicate = lizards$rep)
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > liz.sym <- bilat.symmetry(A = shape, ind = ind, rep = rep, object.sym = TRUE, land.pairs = lizards$lm.pairs, data = gdf, RRPP = TRUE, iter = 149)
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > liz.sym.noRRPP <- bilat.symmetry(A = shape, ind = ind, rep = rep, object.sym = T, land.pairs = lizards$lm.pairs, data = gdf, RRPP = F, iter = 149)
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > summary(liz.sym)
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > summary (liz.sym.noRRPP)
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > #---------------------------------------------------------
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > As can be noted, both ANOVAs have essentially identical results. However, Z values and P values do differ between liz.sym and liz.sym.noRRPP. That there is a difference is, I guess, to be expected, but P values for the inter-individual variation would seem to lead to entirely opposite conclusions. With RRPP, we find P = 0.54, while without it we have P = 0.0066.
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > Considering that the R squared value for inter-individual variation is 0.83, and that the variation explained by digitization error appears much smaller, I would personally be inclined to disregard the result using RRPP, and favor the one not using RRPP. More generally I’d be surprised to find a real biological dataset in which fluctuating asymmetry would be significant while inter-individual variation would not (but who knows?).
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > At the same time, the default behavior of the function is indeed to use RRPP for significance testing, which suggests to me that geomorph authors would tend to favor this option. If someone can confirm that the behavior of the function using RRPP is correct, I’d be interested to understand why this is the case, and how to deal with the interpretation of the results!
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > All the best

1. I found that the difference between two sides calculated for scallop.sym$asym.shapes are asymm.component <- avg.side.symm[indsq,] - avg.side.symm[-indsq,]) (line 329). This is equivalent to (reflection - original) using the scallop data as indisq = [2, 4, 6, 8, 10]

However, the calculation of differences between sides for directional (DA) and fluctuating asymmetry (FA) are all based on (original - reflection). For example, the FA component is:

  FA.component <- ind.mns[-indsq,] - ind.mns[indsq,] #for scallop, it is basically (original - reflection).
  FA.component <- simplify2array(lapply(1:n.ind, function(j)

  {t(matrix(FA.component[j,],k,p)) + mn.shape - mn.DA}))

(lines 341-343)

For example,  using the original bilat.symmtry(), I cannot get the asymmetrical shape of a specimen scallops.sym$asymm.shape[ , , 1] by using FA + DA + grand mean:

scallops.sym$FA.component[, , 1] + (DA.component[, , 1]  - DA.component[, , 2]),

#FA.componet = FA_residual + grand_mean

asymm.component <- avg.side.symm[-indsq,] - avg.side.symm[indsq,])  #In the original function, -indsq and indisq are reversed

Are there any specific reasons for calculating only the overall asymmetrical component as reflection - original, but FA and DA as original - reflections?

2. Why are the asymmetric components directly calculated from the difference between the original and reflection shapes, rather than divided by 2? If we just do (original - reflection), would it calculate left & right difference twice?

Klingenberg 2015 <https://www.mdpi.com/2073-8994/7/2/843> pp. 865 also states that asymmetrical component should be original - symmetrical component, which is 1/2 of original - reflection, and DA = mean original - mean symmetrical = 1/2 * (mean original - mean reflection).

3. Why did the DA.component only export the mean original and reflected shapes? In that case, would it be more straight forward to just export a single DA shape as mn.DA + grand_mean? I feel users can able to calculate left and right mean shape by simply do a mean(asymm.shape).

Thank you very much for your time!

Chi Zhang

Hi Dr. Adams,

Thank you very much for answering my questions. Yes, I agree that some problems are trivial and only about visualizations. And yes, I understand that the directional asymmetry is the mean asymmetry in a sample and the residuals of directional asymmetry can be got from using the scallop.symm$DA.component[, , 1] - scallop.symm$DA.component[, , 2].

I'll go back to read Palmer's original papers about asymmetry to clarify these concepts again.

However, for Klingenberg 2015 I cited, other than the parts I quoted, there is also this "Directional asymmetry is the average of the individual asymmetries and can be computed from the difference of the average of all the original copies minus the overall symmetric consensus in the entire sample (or, equivalent but twice the magnitude, the average shape of all the original minus the average of all the reflected and relabeled copies).

If I read it correctly, it shows that the DA component is (average original - average reflection)/2 = average asymmetry - average symmetry.

For example, for the codes extracted from the bilat.symmetry script using the scallop data https://github.com/chz31/OBIO_689_305_morphometrics/blob/main/test_bilat_asymm.R
In this script, I tried to use the (asymmetry + symmetry) to reconstruct the shape of the first specimen after a pooled GPA of reflections and original configurations.

After running this script, if I do:
specimen1_test <- (asymm.component[, , 1] - mn.shape) + symm.component[, , 1] #line 50
#The asymm.component is calculated from (reflection - original) + mn.shape based on the original bilat.symmetry script
#Thus, this is equivalent to (reflection -original) + symm.component of specimen1
I cannot recover the specimen 1's reflection of the original shape, which is A[, , 6] (because asymm.component is calculated from reflection - original).

However, if I do:
specimen1_test <- (asymm.component[, , 1] - mn.shape)/2 + symm.component[, , 1] #line 54
#I.e., the asymm residual is calculated as (reflection - original)/2
I can actually recover specimen 1's reflection A[, , 6]. Thus, should I consider (reflection - original)/2 (or (original - reflection)/2) as the actual asymmetrical component?

Using (original - reflection) without divided by 2 may still make sense since the 'sides' from ANOVA is just a comparison of average original and average reflection.

Asymmetry components by definition are  the difference between sides. Which comes first is completely arbitrary. R-L and L-R both describe the same FA vector, with the sign reversed. The same for object symmetry. Original – reflection or the opposite is arbitrary decision. There is no a biological nor mathematical  reason that one must precede the other ( the digitizing order of landmarks is completely arbitrary and reversing them would result in this order being reflected).

Klingenberg 2015 inserted an order because one must start somewhere. His downstream sentences follow from his decision of which he started with. That is all.

That being said,  it is inconvenient to have R-L for some components (asymm) and L-R for others (DA and FA). I will make that internally consistent in the next version of geomorph.

Dear Alicia,

Partial correlation is the correlation between variables (or PLS scores) after accounting for the linear association between these and a third variable, for which both are putatively correlated and which is an independent variable, at least for the purpose of estimating the correlation.  For example, if you have Y1 and Y2 as Procrustes coordinates after splitting into two modules, and both module shapes could be associated with organism size, you could find:

R1 <- resid(lm(Y1 ~ size))
R2 <- resid(lm(Y2 ~ size))
pPLS <- two.b.pls(R1, R2)

This will likely yield a different r.pls than PLS <- two.b.pls(Y1, Y2), and the r.pls from the pPLS could be considered a partial correlation coefficient-like result.

What you are describing sounds like you wish to know if you could find clade-specific r.pls scores from a common 2B-PLS analysis?  You could do that by simply finding the Pearson correlation coefficient between subsets of PLS scores.  This might be an interesting thing to do simply to learn if these values tend to differ from the common r.pls found in the PLS object above.  Or, the scores could be used perhaps in a linear model, e.g.,

y <- PLS$YScores[, 1]
x <- PLS$XScores[, 1]

fit <- lm(y ~ clade * x)
anova(fit)

This approach will not tell you what the clade-specific r.pls values are, but if the clade:x effect is significant, it would suggest that the clades have different modular correlations, suggesting it would be better to investigate them clade by clade.

How unfortunate that partial correlations from partial least squares could be called partial-partial least-squares!

Best,
Mike

messages.body_plain:
Colleagues,

We would like to alert you to our new paper on measurement error: “Interrogating Random and Systematic Measurement Error in Morphometric Data”, currently In Press at Evolutionary Biology (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11692-024-09627-6: also available upon request).

Some of you may recall the lively discussion on Morphmet last year regarding the evaluation of ME. This paper is our ‘analytical followup’ to that discussion. The paper provides a thorough overview of the subject as it pertains to morphometric data, and identifies several key issues with its evaluation. First, the commonly used intra-class correlation coefficient (ICC) can be misleading, simply because a greater disparity in shape among observations can inflate ICC estimates. This could lead one to conclude that ME does not introduce concerns for the analysis of shape variation. We demonstrate that reliance on ICC statistics (or R^2 statistics) should be avoided, especially in lieu of explicit hypothesis tests.

Second, we provide a framework for parsing systematic and random components of ME, and performing hypothesis tests for systematic ME.  This hypothesis testing framework can include group-specific evaluation of systematic ME, if data are sampled from different groups that could vary in shape.  We also show via simulation experiments that a consistent digitizing prejudice does not necessarily yield consistent systematic ME among groups, emphasizing the importance of an analytical framework that can detect and pinpoint where issues from digitizing could arise.

Additionally, we provide graphical tools that assist in interpreting which research subjects might be implicated by ME.  We use these statistical and graphical tools to re-analyze a recent example, identifying some cases that could elucidate digitizing issues (and could be revisited).

All of these tools (both statistical and graphical) are available in the latest versions of geomorph and RRPP, now found on CRAN.

Dean Adams and Mike Collyer

Dr. Dean C. Adams

Distinguished Professor of Evolutionary Biology

Department of Ecology, Evolution, and Organismal Biology

Iowa State University

Alicia,

This is definitely (and actually easily) manageable.  I’ll demonstrate with the geomorph example for phylo.intergation.

Here is the example:

data(plethspecies)
Y.gpa <- gpagen(plethspecies$land)    #GPA-alignment
land.gps <- c("A","A","A","A","A","B","B","B","B","B","B")

IT <- phylo.integration(Y.gpa$coords, partition.gp <http://partition.gp> = land.gps,
                        phy = plethspecies$phy)

plot(IT)

which produces this plot:

The red line is the same as a reduced-major axis (RMA) regression, which is actually the same as finding the first PC for the bivariate scores; i.e.,

P <- cbind(IT$XScores[, 1], IT$YScores[, 1])
PCA <- gm.prcomp(P)
plot(PCA)

Notice that the PC plot takes the red line in the previous plot and rotates it to be the abscissa, PC 1, in the second plot.  Therefore, all of the distances to the red line in the first plot are vertical distances from the abscissa in the second plot.  An easy way to calculate these is.

d <- sqrt(PCA$x[, 2]^2)

> d
      P_cinereus P_electromorphus       P_hoffmani      P_hubrichti
    5.766068e-04     1.345735e-03     1.031067e-03     6.584032e-05
      P_nettingi      P_richmondi       P_serratus     P_shenandoah
    3.739870e-04     1.163859e-03     2.464383e-04     9.356576e-04
      P_virginia
    1.017409e-03

Showing you how to do this should not be interpreted as tacit support for doing it.  I am not sure that distance to the RMA fit should be interpreted as something meaningful, like Procrustes distances correspond to amounts of shape change.  I would be careful with using these distances as data that could be analyzed with some other test.

Best,
Mike

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

After digging a bit more in the functions and (re-)reading some of the papers on asymmetry and RRPP, I'd like to come back to the original topic of the thread, which was the bilat.symmetry function.

Firstly, I want to point out that I do understand the major interest of using RRPP in the special case of asymmetry analysis. I do see the P values computed are different in the example I gave in the original post, since the Z values are different with and without RRPP, which makes sense since the pseudo-F values distributions are necessarily going to change due to the difference in resampling pattern.

Despite this, I still find it somehow unsatisfactory that inter-individual variation in the lizard dataset, with an R-sq value of 0.83, and a MS value 6.7 times higher than the sum of the residual and ind:side MS, is found to be "non-significant". And I'd like to reiterate my earlier point about the biological meaningfulness of such result. What would it mean for population shape variation to be "non-significant", while its variance is larger than other components?

Finally, since Mike mentioned that the function is using Type I SS (at least in my example code), would it not make sense to test for side (i.e. directional asymmetry) first, at least in cases where directional asymmetry is large?

Any input or thoughts would be appreciated!

Cheers,
Sam

Le jeudi 1 février 2024 à 16:55:46 UTC+1, mlco...@gmail.com a écrit :
> Dean’s point requires some clarification, I think.
>
> There are two things at play.  First type I SSCPs are used, so the SS for ind would be the same whether using RRPP or FRPP, because the null model has just an intercept, meaning the null model for RRPP simply randomizes values when it randomizes residuals of the global mean.  One might posit that the result should be the same.
>
> However, the second thing is that the F stat is calculated not with respect to residual variance, but the ind:replicate variance.  The distribution for the random SS for this effect will be quite different.  The null model for RRPP is ind + replicate, such that the ind:replicate effect is estimated with ind and replicate effects held constant. >

Every null model has exchangeable units under the null hypothesis, which are typically the residuals (but can be transformed residuals).  Only if a null model is just a mean does randomization of data make sense.  Yet, most permutation tests simply randomize data.  This can be dangerous, and your example sort of suggests why.

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I have some scripts using the function "make_ggplot" to convert plot objects produced from the "plotAllometry" function and they were working just fine. Recently, I updated the geomorph package to the latest version and the following error message appears: "Plot object does not appear to be a type that can be converted to ggplot.".
I was using the R package version 4.2.1, so I updated it to version 4.3.3. I also updated the RStudio. Unfortunately, the same error message appears. I ran the script below, which is an example from the function "make_ggplot" in the geomorph manual from March 2024 and, to my surprise, the same message appeared.
Does any one please have an idea what could be happening?
Here is the script used as example for this function in the manual:

### Allometry example
data(plethodon)
Y.gpa <- gpagen(plethodon$land, print.progress = FALSE) #GPA-alignment
gdf <- geomorph.data.frame(Y.gpa, site = plethodon$site,
species = plethodon$species)
fit <- procD.lm(coords ~ Csize * species * site, data=gdf, iter=0,
print.progress = FALSE)
P <- plotAllometry(fit, size = gdf$Csize, logsz = TRUE, method = "PredLine",
pch = 19, col = as.numeric(interaction(gdf$species, gdf$site)))
make_ggplot(P)

Thanks in advance.
Sincerely,

Daniel

messages.body_plain:
Dear Daniel,

This is an unfortunate result of recent CRAN package publishing stringency with respect to S3 generic functions, forcing the change of $plot.args in the plot objects to $plot_args.  We missed it with make_ggplot, which checks for $plot.args.  We will have to update this.  In the interim, if you do not wish to be stranded, here is a kluge you can use:

P$plot.args <- P$plot_args
make_ggplot(P)

That will duplicate all the plot arguments into a list that make_ggplot recognizes.

Sorry for the inconvenience!

Mike

messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

I just installed R two month ago and I'm relying a lot on the examples uploaded with the packages. I am currently trying to plot a phylomorphospace analysis using gm.prcomp . But when I tried running the example that is comming with the geomorph package, I got an error returned.

Here is the code I used (which are the 15 first line in the example + library) :

library(geomorph)
data(plethspecies)
Y.gpa <- gpagen(plethspecies$land)    #GPA-alignment

###  Traditional PCA
PCA <- gm.prcomp(Y.gpa$coords)
summary(PCA)
plot(PCA, main = "PCA")
plot(PCA, main = "PCA", flip = 1) # flip the first axis
plot(PCA, main = "PCA", axis1 = 3, axis2 = 4) # change PCs viewed

### Phylomorphospace - PCA with phylogeny (result is same as above,
### but with estimated ancestral states projected into plot)
PCA.w.phylo <- gm.prcomp(Y.gpa$coords, phy = plethspecies$phy)
summary(PCA.w.phylo)
plot(PCA.w.phylo, phylo = TRUE, main = "PCA.w.phylo")

And here is the error message (the Tradicional PCA part works just fine) :

> plot(PCA.w.phylo, phylo = TRUE, main = "PCA.w.phylo") Erreur : Some of the arguments in phylo.pars are different than those that are possible (see Arguments).

But it still plotted a graph, just without the phylogeny on it (attached in copy).

Is it a problem in my code that can be solved ? because i didn't touch the data so i dont really see why it would have different arguments than those that are possible...

Thank you for your time !
Célian.

messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

I want to compare variance of shape at different developmental stages in pairwise manner to see if there is difference in variance between them.

Code I used looks similar to this:
morphol.disparity(coords~stage, groups = stage , iter = 999)

where function returns Procrustes variance for each group, pairwise absolute differences and the P-values obtained from permutation tests. To my understanding, this way I am comparing the spread of coordinates from the mean of their corresponding stage.

I am uncertain do I compare the obtained P-values to the threshold of 0.05 or I should perform adjustment for multiple testing based on the number of stages I have. Any insight is welcome!

Kind regards,
Marko
